lines: Take a writer sealing one new file every so often, on a stream that never stops arriving.
Make it seal a new file twice as often, on that exact same total amount of data.
Roughly twice as many files come out the other end, for the identical data.
Every approach covered up to this point eventually had to produce an actual result.
Somewhere, a person or another system needs to be able to ask a real question of it.
This part of the picture is the first of the two places that result actually lands.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
Seal a new file twice as often as before, over that same stretch of time.
On that same total amount of incoming data, what happens to how many files come out?
answer: It roughly doubles, and here's exactly why.
Each sealed batch now only covers about half as much data as it used to.
Covering that same total amount of data again just takes about twice as many of them.

lines: Seal a batch twice as often, and each one only covers about half the data it used to.
Covering that same total amount of data again takes about twice as many sealed batches.
How soon a given write becomes visible also shrinks by about that same half.
One path turns the raw flow into a table completely automatically, nothing built by hand at all.
A separate path reaches that exact same kind of table by running a hand-written job instead.
Both end up putting the same result in the same place, built two very different ways.
A job like that only ever makes a write durable at its own periodic checkpoint.
Sealing a batch into the table turns out to ride on that very same checkpoint.
So shortening one of those two settings is really just shortening the other, not a separate choice.
Worth reasoning through once more before this reveal settles it.
Sealing more often always costs more of these small files, on the writing side alone.
What could soak up all those small, frequent files without slowing that sealing down at all?
answer: Something sitting underneath that quietly merges them back together, and here's how.
A storage layer that buffers whatever lands on it, then merges it on its own schedule.
The sealing itself never has to slow down for that merging to happen.

lines: Keep that exact same frequent sealing rhythm from before, completely unchanged.
Run everything it produces through a layer that buffers and then merges it back together.
What lands on disk at the end shrinks down to a small fraction of the unmerged version.
One kind of storage keeps its own internal structure built specifically for frequent small updates.
A separate, newer kind of storage sits directly in front of the stream processor itself.
Both of those answer the exact same underlying question, just from the storage side instead of the writer's.
An automatic path, a hand-built path, and a storage-side path were all just covered in turn.
Every single one of them still has to put that same cost down somewhere.
None of the three ever actually makes that underlying cost disappear outright.
Every number in this reel came from one real run, happening just now, of this topic's own toy model.
The sealing frequency that really did double the files and really did halve how long a write stays stale.
That same exact sealing rhythm, merged afterward, that really did land only a small fraction of those files.
So: sealing more often always buys freshness and always costs more small files, together, every time.
An automatic path, a hand-built path, or a storage-side path can each carry that one cost.
Not one of them removes it. One destination was covered here; a very different one comes next.
